The B+ tree part is overstated. InnoDB stores rows in a clustered B+ tree, but PostgreSQL stores rows in a heap with B-tree indexes, and LSM engines (RocksDB, Cassandra) write tombstones. InnoDB does not rebalance on each DELETE: the row is delete-marked and physically removed later by background purge, and pages merge only when a page falls below MERGE_THRESHOLD (50% full by default). In PostgreSQL a DELETE leaves a dead tuple for VACUUM. Soft-delete UPDATEs also write to every index that contains is_deleted.
precise_version: Engines defer the physical work of a delete (InnoDB purge, PostgreSQL VACUUM) and merge index pages only when they fall below a fill threshold, so a hard delete does not trigger a rebalance each time. Choose soft delete for recovery, archival and audit, not as a B+ tree optimisation.

note: A soft delete leaves the row's key in place, but it is still a write: InnoDB treats an UPDATE of an indexed column as delete-mark plus insert in that secondary index, and PostgreSQL's MVCC writes a new row version (UPDATE 'does not immediately remove the old version'). The saving over a hard delete is smaller than 'no rebalancing'.

Rows in mainstream row stores are not fixed-width once they have variable-length columns. InnoDB's record header 'contains the lengths of variable-length columns'; a fixed-length header only applies when all columns are NOT NULL and fixed length. VARCHAR stores length + data (L+1 or L+2 bytes). Offsets are computed from the header, not from a fixed layout.
precise_version: Row stores keep a row's columns together; fixed-length columns sit at known offsets, while variable-length columns (VARCHAR) are found through length fields in the record header, so rows are generally variable length.

note: The C struct analogy only holds for fixed-length columns (INT, CHAR, DATETIME); variable-length columns break fixed offsets (see L-0190).
Usually true, but in InnoDB DYNAMIC format long VARCHAR values can also go off-page: 'When a row is too long, the longest columns are chosen for off-page storage.'

Engine-dependent. InnoDB DYNAMIC: TEXT/BLOB values of 40 bytes or less are stored inline, and longer values move off-page (20-byte pointer) only when the row does not fit the page. PostgreSQL makes no short/long type distinction: TOAST compresses or moves any value out of line once the row is over ~2 kB.

Off-page values do cost extra page reads (possibly several overflow pages), but these are usually buffer-pool hits, not disk calls. They are only paid when the column is selected: PostgreSQL pulls TOASTed values out only 'if selected at all'.
MySQL: InnoDB's max in-page row size is 'slightly less than 8KB for the default 16KB page size'; TEXT/BLOB count only 9-12 bytes toward the row limit because their contents are stored separately.

What the teacher upheld (batching hard deletes rebalances less) overstates how engines work. InnoDB already defers physical removal to background purge and merges a page only when it drops below MERGE_THRESHOLD, so per-row deletes do not each trigger a rebalance. Batching mainly saves transaction, lock and log overhead.
Same issue as L-0228: page merges depend on page fill (default below 50%), not on how many DELETE statements you group. Grouping reduces commit and locking overhead.

Batching in chunks (e.g. DELETE ... LIMIT N, repeated) is the right practice, and MySQL recommends it 'to ensure that a given DELETE statement does not take too much time'. But the benefit is not '1 rebalance per 100 rows': it is shorter lock time, smaller transactions and less log flushing.
precise_version: Deleting in batches (e.g. 100 rows per commit) cuts per-transaction lock, commit and log overhead; index page merges still happen only when pages fall below their fill threshold.

note: The overflow concern is real (signed 32-bit max 2,147,483,647, which is 19 Jan 2038 as epoch seconds), but the next step is a 64-bit integer (bigint), not a double. Epoch milliseconds already need 64 bits today, and 64-bit epoch seconds do not overflow in any practical horizon.

A signed 4-byte epoch-seconds counter overflows on 19 January 2038 03:14:07 UTC (the 'Year 2038' limit, which is also the end of MySQL TIMESTAMP's range), not 2032. An unsigned 32-bit counter lasts until 2106.
precise_version: A signed 32-bit epoch-seconds value runs out on 19 January 2038; moving to 64 bits doubles the size but removes the limit.

note: Negative epoch values are normal and well supported: MongoDB's BSON Date 'is signed. Negative values represent dates before 1970', with a range of about 290 million years either side. Signed integers handle pre-1970 dates fine; the real constraint is width (see L-0232).
Teacher hedged ('let's say'). MySQL (5.6.4+) DATETIME takes 5 bytes plus 0-3 bytes for fractional seconds (8 bytes at microsecond precision); TIMESTAMP 4 bytes; DATE 3 bytes.

MySQL's range is much narrower: DATETIME supports '1000-01-01 00:00:00' to '9999-12-31 23:59:59' (no BCE dates), and TIMESTAMP only 1970-2038. The wide range the teacher recalls matches PostgreSQL: timestamp spans 4713 BC to 294276 AD in 8 bytes.
precise_version: MySQL DATETIME packs years 1000-9999 into 5 bytes; PostgreSQL's 8-byte timestamp covers 4713 BC to 294276 AD.

MySQL recommends DELETE ... LIMIT row_count, repeated, 'to ensure that a given DELETE statement does not take too much time', and warns that large deletes can exceed InnoDB's lock table size.

A DELETE already takes row locks inside its transaction; you do not need to lock first to prevent stale reads. The interviewer's real concern is lock duration and contention from a large delete, which affects latency and availability. That is why chunked deletes are advised.

The conflict is real, but hard delete is not the only fix. PostgreSQL supports partial unique indexes (CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... WHERE condition), so uniqueness can apply only to rows that are not deleted. In MySQL a common workaround is to include a deleted marker/timestamp in the unique key.
precise_version: Soft delete conflicts with plain unique indexes; fix it with a partial unique index (e.g. unique on email WHERE NOT is_deleted) or by hard deleting.
